newsitem.title: UK: Arab paper gets letter bombs at London, UN offices.
newsitem.headline: Arab paper gets letter bombs at London, UN offices.

text.p: A letter bomb exploded in the London office of the Al-Hayat newspaper on Monday, injuring two security guards, and a second letter bomb was found in the U.N. building in New York, addressed to the paper's office there.
British police said four more suspect devices were found at the London office of the Saudi-owned Arab-language daily, but were made safe with controlled explosions.
One of the injured security guards, Briton Barry Roach, 46, was reported to have been holding the package when it went off at around 0910 GMT.
He received face and abdominal injuries and, although his condition was stable, doctors at Charing Cross Hospital in west London said he could lose an eye.
His colleague, Andy McKenzie, 35, was discharged after being treated for shock and damaged eardrums.
The New York bomb was found in a messenger room at the United Nations headquarters in New York, a U.N. spokesman said. A second suspicious envelope was being examined.
Security guards evacuated and closed off parts of the press area at the U.N. complex and the New York police bomb squad was called in.

U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said the bomb sent to the United Nations was in a greeting-card sized envelope addressed to Al-Hayat -- similar to several devices mailed earlier this month to the newspaper's Washington bureau.
"It is a live bomb and it is going to be exploded (under controlled conditions) in the basement," he said.
The Saudi ambassador in London issued a statement condemning the British bombs.
"This is a criminal, cowardly act which illustrates the mentality of the perpetrators," said ambassador Ghazi Algosaibi. "Those who cannot face ideas resort to bombs."
Al-Hayat editor Jihad Khazen said the attack had come without warning. "Nobody threatened us or demanded anything."

The FBI is conducting an international investigation after eight letter bombs made to look like Christmas cards were mailed from Egypt to the United States. The bureau warned that there may be more bombs in the mail.

None of the potentially lethal devices exploded. Five were addressed to Al-Hayat in Washington -- four arrived and one was found in the postal system -- and three turned up in the area around Leavenworth federal prison in Kansas.
Khazen said the bomb that exploded at his office carried a postmark from Alexandria in Egypt, as did some of those found in the U.S.

The FBI has dismissed as "speculative" reports it is investigating a possible connection between the letter bombs and the 1993 bombing of the World Trade Centre and a foiled plot to bomb other New York landmarks.

Mohamed Salameh, a militant Moslem jailed for life for the World Trade Centre bombing, is in Leavenworth, as is Victor Alvarez, convicted of plotting to blow up the United Nations headquarters and other New York targets.
U.S. media reports said the letter bombs found there were made of Semtex plastic explosive. Police were not immediately able to specify the kind of explosive used in London.
Al-Hayat, which is published in London, is a moderate voice in Arab politics.
"We have been criticising extremism in the Arab world for the last eight years. I hope and pray there will be no more attacks. We will not change," Kazen said.
